source.title_on_document: The Crowdless Future? Generative AI and Creative Problem-Solving

paper_design_summary: The authors ran a crowdsourcing challenge for circular-economy business ideas (125 eligible human solutions) and had one author prompt GPT-4 to generate 730 solutions under two configurations (multiple independent instances vs. a single instance told to differentiate each new answer). A random selection of 54 human-crowd and 180 GPT-4 solutions was rated blind by 300 screened Prolific evaluators, each randomly assigned to one of 18 blocks of 13 solutions, on novelty, strategic viability, environmental value, financial value, and overall quality. No person was assigned to work with or without AI; the comparison is AI-generated output versus human output.

studies.label: Human crowd vs. GPT-4 (human-prompted) solutions to a circular-economy business-idea challenge, rated by 300 evaluators

assignment.what_was_assigned: Evaluators (raters) were randomly assigned to one of 18 blocks of solutions; the 234 rated solutions were randomly selected from the pool. No person was assigned to AI assistance: human-crowd solutions were written without AI and the human-AI solutions were generated by one author prompting GPT-4.
assignment.quote: each evaluator was randomly assigned one of the 18 blocks of solutions to evaluate; that is, evaluators were nested within solution blocks.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1596), Evaluator Recruitment and Procedures; Figure 2, PDF p. 10 (journal p. 1597)

arms.name: Human crowd (HC)
arms.description: Solutions submitted by human solvers to the crowdsourcing challenge on Freelancer.com; 54 of 125 eligible solutions randomly selected for rating

arms.name: HAI multiple instance (independent search)
arms.description: GPT-4 solutions, each from a distinct GPT-4 instance with the same prompt (one of three prompt-engineering approaches); 90 rated

arms.name: HAI single instance (differentiated search)
arms.description: GPT-4 solutions generated successively in one instance with an instruction to tackle a different problem and propose a different solution each time; 90 rated

participants.exclusions: Creators: the contest received 310 submissions; 148 participants received $10 for nonblank entries; the team deemed 125 of the 148 submissions eligible after removing off-topic or insufficiently detailed ones; 54 HC solutions were randomly selected for rating (the paper does not state the number of distinct solvers behind the 54). GPT-4 solutions: 730 generated, 180 randomly selected (90 per configuration). Raters: 1,000 Prolific evaluators recruited, 300 passed the screening survey and rated (145 July 2023, 155 September 2023).
participants.who: Human-crowd solvers: 'global solvers from various industries' responding to a challenge run with Continuum Laboratory and Freelancer.com. Raters (not creators): 300 US Prolific workers screened for interest, work experience, and circular-economy knowledge.
participants.country: Solvers: global (countries not listed); raters: United States
participants.quote: The challenge attracted 125 global solvers from various industries, and we used strategic prompt engineering to generate the human-AI solutions. We recruited 300 external human evaluators to judge a randomized selection of 13 out of 234 solutions
participants.locator: PDF p. 2 (journal p. 1589), Abstract; PDF p. 8 (journal p. 1595), Crowdsourcing Context; PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1596), Evaluator Recruitment and Procedures

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 via the Python API, default temperature 1.0
ai_tool.how_used: One of the study's authors wrote prompts (baseline problem description with one-shot example and evaluation criteria; role-play with solver characteristics; role-play with expert personas from 23 industries) and GPT-4 generated complete solutions in either multiple independent instances or a single instance with differentiation instructions. No study participant used AI.

task.description: Propose a sustainable, circular-economy business idea in problem-solution format, judged on novelty, strategic viability, environmental value, financial value, and overall quality.
task.duration: Challenge ran January 30 to May 15, 2023; GPT-4 took 27.2 seconds per solution on average; the paper states HC solutions took 2,520 hours and HAI solutions 5.5 hours in total.

outcomes.name: Novelty rating
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Five-point Likert rating by screened Prolific evaluators blind to source: 'How different is it from existing solutions?' Nested mixed-effects models (lmerTest) with random effects for evaluators and blocks, controls for screening criteria, evaluator demographics, cohort, and word count. Variant: Top Novelty (binary, rating of 5): HAI vs HC -0.079 (0.012), p < 0.001 (Table 5); multiple -0.091 (0.014), single -0.065 (0.014), both p < 0.001 (Table 6). Top-decile means HC 4.364, multiple 3.901, single 4.003 (Table 2). Models without controls are in Appendix D (online, not read).

company_involvement.description: The challenge was run in partnership with Continuum Laboratory (an AI firm) and Freelancer.com. Coauthor Vladimir Jacimovic is affiliated with ContinuumLab.AI and described as its CEO and founder. Funding came from Harvard Business School and LISH.

eligibility.reason: No person was randomly assigned to AI assistance. The paper compares solutions written by a human crowd without AI against solutions generated by GPT-4 from one author's prompts; randomization applies only to which solutions were rated and which block each of 300 raters saw. On the AI side a single person produced all prompts, so there is no group of people working with AI to count toward 50. Outcomes are blind human ratings of the outputs, which would satisfy criterion 3.

one_line_finding: In blind ratings (300 evaluators, 3,900 ratings), GPT-4 solutions scored lower than human-crowd solutions on novelty (-0.140, SE 0.035) but higher on strategic viability (0.088), environmental value (0.160), financial value (0.143), and overall quality (0.101, SE 0.032) (Table 3, p. 1599); the single-instance differentiated configuration closed the novelty gap (-0.056, p = 0.156; Table 4, p. 1600).
open_questions: Construct of the 'Quality' rating: coded overall_creativity because raters judged overall quality across novelty and the three value criteria; the codebook also lists 'quality' under usefulness.
Whether 'mixed' is the right value for ai_available_when_produced in an ai_vs_human comparison (HC written without AI, HAI produced by GPT-4).
Appendix E (text analysis of HC and HAI solutions, possibly including similarity or diversity measures) is in the online supplement, not in this PDF; it was not read.
notes: Participant counts: the paper gives 125 eligible human solvers (abstract) and 148 participants paid for nonblank entries, but only 54 HC solutions were rated and the paper does not state how many distinct solvers they come from, so people counts are left null; solution counts per arm (54/90/90) are in Table 2. The 300 evaluators are raters, not creators. Possible inconsistencies in the document: (1) text on p. 1597 says quality for single instance exceeds HC with p = 0.011, while Table 2 prints p = 0.007 for single vs HC and 0.011 for single vs multiple; (2) Table 6 Model 2 prints SE (0.031) for HAI Multiple Instance, much larger than the other top-rating SEs (0.011-0.015). Table 2 parenthesized values are unlabeled (presumably SDs). Table notes print '****p < 0.1'. Raters were screened for circular-economy interest, experience, or knowledge, but the paper itself calls them crowd rather than domain experts, so measure is coded human_raters. Pages are PDF pages; PDF p. 1 is the INFORMS cover and PDF p. N = journal p. N + 1587.
